title: Large format holograms as wall art

posts.topic_title: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.post_subject: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.content_md:
I have a couple of large holograms hanging in my living room. They really are a very large black surface for most of the time. Unless you are in just the right spot (they are H2 reflections) the are totally black. What have people done to try to make the more interesting?

I have a hologram that has a picture as a background. It really is not very interesting. Could one record a low frequency grating that has a wide field of view without compromising the main image? I am thinking of something more like a rainbow until you hit the right spot then you only see the main image. But, I am not sure how to make it.

What other ideas are there?

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.post_subject: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.content_md: How about lighting with more than one spotlight, angles separated so that the viewing cones from each spot barely overlap? I just checked this with a flashlight on one of my wall H2s and it looks like it should work. 3 spots would at least triple the viewing angle. Thanks for asking this - I might never have thought of this as a problem to be solved otherwise.

posts.topic_title: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.content_md:
I think you've voiced one of the main reasons why holography hasn't been accepted in the general public. Even when properly installed and lit, it's very difficult to find holograms (especially large ones) which fit easily into home decor. 

The light source needed to make the hologram work its magic is essentially an intense highlight. The use of LEDs makes the hologram look better, but not the wall (too saturated in my opinion). Veiling reflections can easily compete with the image, especially during the daytime. And as you point out, the object is essentially a black plate with grey "swirrels" on it when viewed outside the viewing zone.

The best solution I've seen is when holograms are incorporated into sculpture, instead of being framed and put on the wall. It's a more appropriate setting for the three dimensional imagery, because sculpture makes a much better interface between the holographic space recorded and the real world around it. 

For the wall, however, I think the "Portholes" made by Laser Reflections is the best solution I've seen for image-planed reflection holograms. Also, Denisyuk holograms work much better on the wall because of their super-wide viewing zone. I like Nancy Gorglione's sculpturally framed work as well (I'd call it visual jazz). Certainly there are other examples, but none would simply be framed flat plates.

One of the main reasons I explore the avenue of Denisyuks and ultimately DCG is the viewing angle. I never likes 4 x 5 holograms made from 4 x 5 or 8 x 10 masters because the viewing angle is too small. I feel a 16 x 20 master should be used for making 4 by 5 copies.

My single beam DCG reflection holograms are not only viewable from any angle but are "bright" (viewable at least) even when the spot light is not on them.

posts.topic_title: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.content_md:
[quote:db85c0b116]I am thinking of something more like a rainbow until you hit the right spot then you only see the main image. But, I am not sure how to make it. [/quote:db85c0b116]

Couldn't you make a low frequency grating on a larger film/glass than your display hologram then cover the grating film/glass with a piece of material, such as saran wrap, just exactly the size of your display hologram before you develop such that the developer does not interact with the grating over the covered area. ? If the grating does not develop in the area of your display piece, then no fringes - no diffraction. There may be some light thrown into the direction of the image of the display piece, but by making the grating weak or restricting the angles this may not matter too much. Another problem may be that if you don't fix, then the undeveloped area will print out and go black, but if the grating is placed behind a display hologram which is already blacked at the back, it won't matter. 

Another scheme may be to have lots of small gratings and tile around the display piece.

Yet another is to get an artist friend (you do have artist friends, right?) to paint a large painting/wall mural and leave a piece out of the middle. Maybe even involve the black area of the hologram and create an effect such that the black area of the unlit hologram is an integral part of the painting, but takes on another "integral role" when the hologram is illuminated. 

And yet another is... OK, OK, I'll stop now!

posts.topic_title: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.content_md:
To increase the viewing zone of a "subject" hologram, how about making a a double exposure HOE as follows:

A) a common reference beam diverges from a point at normal incidence and a distance equal to the H1 to H2 distance of the "subject" hologram,

B) the first exposure "object" beam diverges from a point off to the right and at the same distance as the reference beam and in the horizontal plane, 

C) the second exposure "object" beam diverges from a point off to the left and at the same distance as the reference beam and also in the horizontal plane, and

D) the resulting HOE is placed in front on the "subject" hologram for display.

The effect is that the image (viewing zone) reconstructed by the "subject" hologram becomes the conjugate of the reference beam of the HOE, which then diffracts the image into two similar images off to the sides. I remember making this a very long time ago and honestly can't remember where the idea came from (it may be published somewhere), but it did work. The horizontal distance between the reference and "object" point sources should equal the width of the viewing zone of the "subject" hologram.

posts.content_md:
So let me try to undertand this. You make a transmission HOE with one object beam and two reference beams, or vice versa. In a HOE it doesn;t matter which is object and which is reference. Basically:

shot 1: diverging beam from middle and one from right. Same side of plate

shot 2: diverging beam from middle and one from left. Same side of plate

Place this HOE in front of a previously made reflection hologram. The reconstruction of the previously made hologram goes through the HOE and hits the hologram. The returned, reconstructed object beam now goes through the HOE and diffracts left and right, since the reconstructed object beam forms the reference for the HOE. Correct?

If this is so, wouldn't it cause massive distortions in the reconstructed reflection hologram, unless the H2 were originally made with the correct angle matched to the HOE. Ah, I think I begin to see it! You have to match. Then one is pseudo and one is ortho. One diverges and one concverges. Clever!

posts.topic_title: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: Large format holograms as wall art
posts.content_md:
> The returned, reconstructed object beam now goes through the HOE and diffracts left and right, since the reconstructed object beam forms the reference for the HOE. Correct?

Correct, except your sentence should read "since the reconstructed object beam forms the *reconstruction* for the HOE" at normal incidence.

> wouldn't it cause massive distortions in the reconstructed reflection hologram, unless the H2 were originally made with the correct angle matched to the HOE.

The reconstruction beam for the "subject" hologram comes in from the top and therefore goes right on through the HOE without modification (because it's way off Bragg for the HOE, it only diffracts horizontally). The reconstructed object of the "subject" hologram is the H1, which is at the same distance from the H2 as the HOE's reference point source (and both are at normal incidence). The H1 is then imaged to the left and right, which means the image at the H1 plane is also seen (undistorted) to the left and right. 

The HOE must be of very high transparency and diffraction efficiency. Maybe someone on the forum can identify the originator of this technique, it wasn't me. Possibly Steve Benton, early to mid '80s?
